questions.stem: Adebayo, who selects investments for the state-owned fund NI, quickly decides that NI should fund an urban infrastructure project before a mining project, without apparent analysis of either. The sequence supports the party currently in power and defers the mining project until the opposition may take control, and she also believes the urban project may be more profitable in the short term. Adebayo's decision is most likely a violation of:

options.A: Suitability.
options.B: Diligence and Reasonable Basis.
options.C: No Standard.

rationales.A: An urban infrastructure project is consistent with NI's socioeconomic purpose, so mandate fit is not where this decision fails and Standard III(C) Suitability is not the standard tested. What is missing is any investment analysis at all: Adebayo decides quickly and on political grounds, which is a failure of diligence and reasonable basis under Standard V(A).
rationales.B: Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis requires members to exercise diligence, independence, and thoroughness, as well as to have a reasonable and adequate basis to support investment action. Adebayo's decision to invest quickly, without apparent analysis, is made on political rather than investment or financial considerations. She is facing political pressures from senior governmental supporters of each project: sequencing the urban project first supports the party currently in power, and postponing the mining project pushes it toward a period when the opposition may hold control. She must thoroughly and independently investigate each potential investment and be resolute in maintaining her independence and objectivity so as to act in the best interests of NI and its investors.
rationales.C: Sovereign or state ownership does not place an investment decision outside the Code and Standards; NI's investment staff remain bound by them whatever the political setting. A quick, politically driven decision taken without analysis fails Standard V(A), so there is a violation.

questions.stem: NI's mandate requires it to invest in projects that offer both a beneficial socioeconomic impact and a positive expected investment return, and its investors are informed up front that investment return is not the single determining factor in its decisions. When Corrales asks Adebayo for detailed information ahead of a hedge fund investment in NI, she provides the standard investor disclosure package; when the fund's partners then press for assurances that NI will maintain an aggressive strategy and a commitment to high returns, Adebayo assures them that NI is committed to providing investors with high rates of return. Adebayo's assurance is most likely a violation of:

options.A: Misrepresentation only.
options.B: Suitability.
options.C: No Standard.

rationales.A: The objection is not simply that Adebayo overstated expected returns to the hedge fund partners. What makes the assurance improper is that it commits NI to something its mandate does not permit, and taking action or making promises inconsistent with a specific mandate is the suitability failure of Standard III(C) rather than a bare misstatement under Standard I(C).
rationales.B: Standard III(C) Suitability requires members responsible for managing assets to a specific mandate, strategy, or style to take only investment actions that are consistent with that mandate. In the case of NI, Adebayo has a dual mandate to invest in projects that have both a beneficial socioeconomic impact and a positive expected investment return. That dual mandate is in contrast to traditional investment mandates, which focus only on return on investment regardless of outside or other impact, and NI's investors are informed up front that investment return is not the single determining factor for NI's investment decisions. Any assurances by Adebayo to the hedge fund or to other investors that promise a set rate of return or prioritize return maximization would be contrary to NI's mandate.
rationales.C: Delivering the standard investor disclosure package discharges disclosure mechanics but it does not license assurances that conflict with the mandate being managed. Adebayo's promise of high rates of return sets return maximization above NI's dual mandate of socioeconomic impact plus positive expected return, so Standard III(C) is violated whatever the disclosure package contained.

questions.stem: After the hedge fund he manages decides to invest in NI, Corrales immediately invests 25% of his personal portfolio in NI in return for shares, before the fund makes its own investment. Once the fund's investment is made public, NI shares trade higher on the exchange. Corrales's personal purchase is most likely a violation of:

options.A: Priority of Transactions.
options.B: Disclosure of Conflicts.
options.C: No Standard.

rationales.A: Corrales engaged in the unethical and often illegal practice of front-running, that is, trading in advance for one's personal account prior to trading for client accounts for economic advantage. Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions states that investment transactions for clients must have priority over investment transactions for personal benefit. After the hedge fund invests in NI, the value of NI shares increases, benefiting Corrales through an increase in the value of his personal investment. The practice is unethical and violates Standard VI(B) even if his personal investment does not disadvantage the hedge fund in any way. Corrales should have waited to invest in NI until after the hedge fund had completed its investment.
rationales.B: Standard VI(A) would require Corrales to disclose a personal stake that could impair his objectivity, but disclosure would not cure what he did here. He bought ahead of a client transaction he knew was coming, and the requirement that client transactions take priority over personal ones sits in Standard VI(B), not in the conflict-disclosure standard.
rationales.C: That Corrales committed his own capital and bore his own risk does not excuse buying ahead of the fund's known pending investment. That is front-running, and it violates Standard VI(B) even where the fund suffers no disadvantage, because client transactions must come first.

questions.stem: Corrales engages local subadvisers who have minimal investment experience but close connections with high-ranking local officials. The subadvisers are paid "deal fees" to cover expenses incurred in facilitating governmental support, Corrales does not require details of the activities those fees pay for, and he reports the payments to the hedge fund's investors as operating expenses. Corrales's conduct is most likely a violation of:

options.A: Diligence and Reasonable Basis.
options.B: Independence and Objectivity.
options.C: Misrepresentation.

rationales.A: The subadvisers' lack of investment experience is a genuine concern, but it is not what this item turns on. The reported treatment of the payments is: describing undocumented connection payments as legitimate hedge fund operating expenses misstates the nature of the fund's costs to its investors, which is Standard I(C) Misrepresentation, with Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law implicated by the nature of the arrangement itself.
rationales.B: Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity addresses gifts, benefits, and pressures that could compromise a member's own judgment. Here the officials' connections are what is being purchased, and the violation tested is the misrepresentation of those payments in reports to investors under Standard I(C), not a compromise of Corrales's own objectivity in selecting the subadvisers.
rationales.C: By reporting subadvisory payments as legitimate hedge fund operating expenses, Corrales is misrepresenting the nature of the payments in order to hide illegal activity, in violation of Standard I(C) Misrepresentation. Although it is acceptable to hire subadvisers to assist in sourcing investment opportunities, Corrales is not hiring a subadviser to assist in the investment decision-making process; he is essentially engaged in bribery and in facilitating local corruption. The deal fees are corrupt transactions and are not supported by any documentation detailing legitimate investment expenses. Such conduct violates multiple standards: Corrales very likely also violates Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law, because his conduct would most likely violate applicable anti-bribery laws.

questions.stem: Adebayo continues to use the CFA designation on her business card and in marketing materials even though she has stopped paying her CFA Institute dues, telling a colleague that the credential is like a university degree that cannot be taken away, and during a sales presentation she states that NI's senior investment professionals are all CFA charterholders. Adebayo's conduct is most likely a violation of:

options.A: Reference to the CFA Designation.
options.B: No Standard.
options.C: Knowledge of the Law.

rationales.A: Standard VII(B) Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program states that when referring to the CFA designation, members and candidates must not misrepresent holding the designation. The CFA designation is not like a degree from a university: once granted the right to use the designation, individuals must also satisfy CFA Institute membership requirements, including paying dues and submitting a Professional Conduct Statement annually, to maintain the right to refer to themselves as CFA charterholders. Although Adebayo earned her charter, her membership is considered lapsed because she has not been paying her dues. Until her membership is reactivated she must not use the CFA designation or present herself as a charterholder to potential investors, although she may state that she was previously a CFA Institute member.
rationales.B: Having legitimately earned the charter by passing the exams is not enough to keep using the designation. Membership lapses when dues go unpaid, and with it the right to present oneself as a charterholder in the present tense, so her business card, marketing materials, and presentation statement all misrepresent her status under Standard VII(B).
rationales.C: Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law concerns applicable laws and regulations governing professional activities, not the terms on which CFA Institute membership is maintained. Misrepresenting active charterholder status is addressed directly by Standard VII(B).

questions.stem: Mehrotra knows that Adebayo's CFA Institute membership has lapsed for unpaid dues, yet he says nothing when she tells a prospective investor that NI's senior investment professionals are all CFA charterholders. Mehrotra's silence is most likely a violation of:

options.A: Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs.
options.B: Knowledge of the Law.
options.C: No Standard.

rationales.A: Standard VII(A) governs a member's own conduct as a participant in CFA Institute programs, such as exam confidentiality and program integrity, and it is not what Mehrotra's silence offends. The operative requirement is Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law, which prohibits knowingly participating or assisting in the violations of others and requires dissociation from unethical or illegal conduct.
rationales.B: Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law prohibits members from knowingly participating or assisting in the violations of others and requires members to dissociate from any unethical or illegal conduct. Mehrotra's acquiescence and silence during Adebayo's misrepresentation to the client, at minimum, assists Adebayo's violation of the standard. By keeping silent about false information given to a potential investor, when doing so is potentially harmful to that investor, Mehrotra's behavior constitutes assisting in the violations of those who provide that false information, even where there is no active conduct by Mehrotra himself.
rationales.C: Making no false statement of his own does not clear Mehrotra. He knew the statement to the client was false, and knowing silence in that situation is participation in, or assistance with, another member's violation; Standard I(A) obliges him to dissociate from it.

questions.stem: At a post-exam celebration, Mehrotra, who teaches a CFA exam preparatory class, asks his students for their opinions on which exam questions were the most difficult, hoping to use the information to help ensure that future students are better prepared. Mehrotra's conduct is most likely a violation of:

options.A: No Standard.
options.B: Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs.
options.C: Knowledge of the Law.

rationales.A: Candidates cannot provide specific information about the exam regarding the questions or the subjects tested within a topic area, and Mehrotra violated Standard VII(A) by soliciting information about specific exam questions. That collecting post-exam feedback is common practice among exam-prep instructors does not make the solicitation permissible, and the intention of preparing future students better does not change what is being sought: confidential exam content.
rationales.B: Standard VII(A) Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs protects the integrity and confidentiality of the exam. Candidates cannot provide specific information about the exam regarding the questions or the subjects tested within a topic area. Mehrotra violated Standard VII(A) by soliciting information about specific exam questions, and the violation lies in the solicitation itself, whether or not the students answered him and whatever use he intended to make of what they said.
rationales.C: Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law concerns applicable laws and regulations. Conduct that undermines the integrity or confidentiality of CFA Institute exams is governed directly by Standard VII(A), which is the standard Mehrotra's solicitation breaches.

questions.stem: Mehrotra tells candidates in his later preparatory classes that his previous students found the CFA exam more difficult than they had expected, in order to emphasize the need to prepare thoroughly. Mehrotra's conduct is most likely:

options.A: No violation, because he waited until results were released.
options.B: A violation, because all post-exam commentary is confidential.
options.C: No violation, because general impressions of difficulty may be shared.

rationales.A: Nothing here turns on timing, and no rule ties the sharing of students' impressions to the release of exam results. General impressions of exam difficulty may be shared because they convey no confidential exam content, whether results have been published or not. What Standard VII(A) prohibits is disclosing specific questions, the subjects tested, or the broader topic areas, and that prohibition does not expire when results come out.
rationales.B: Not all post-exam commentary is confidential. General difficulty impressions are permitted commentary; only specific exam content is confidential, namely the questions themselves and the subjects tested within a topic area. Telling later classes that previous students found the exam harder than expected reveals none of that, so there is nothing for Standard VII(A) to prohibit.
rationales.C: Candidates may generally disclose whether they believed the CFA exam was difficult relative to their expectations. It is acceptable for Mehrotra to advise future preparatory classes that his previous students found the CFA exam to be more difficult than expected and that students should therefore study as much as possible and prepare thoroughly. No specific question, and no subject tested within a topic area, is revealed by a general statement about difficulty, so Standard VII(A) is not breached.

questions.stem: Hockett's team at BankGlobal acts on the firm's analysts' recommendation changes for its discretionary accounts before those changes are publicly disseminated to all of the firm's clients. The team's practice is most likely a violation of:

options.A: Material Nonpublic Information.
options.B: Fair Dealing.
options.C: No Standard.

rationales.A: A pending change in the firm's own recommendation is not material nonpublic information about an issuer, so Standard II(A) is not the standard at issue; a firm may act on its own research. What it may not do is serve some clients ahead of others, which makes this a fair dealing question under Standard III(B).
rationales.B: By acting on the analysts' recommendation changes for their discretionary accounts before the changes are publicly disseminated, the team is violating Standard III(B) Fair Dealing. Standard III(B) requires members and candidates to deal fairly and objectively with all clients when providing investment analysis, making investment recommendations, taking investment action, or engaging in other professional activities. Hockett's team is not treating all BankGlobal clients in a fair and impartial manner: Hockett is giving preferential treatment to his discretionary accounts at the expense of other clients, who receive the recommendation change only after the team has already traded on it.
rationales.C: Discretionary authority settles whether the team may trade without consulting the client; it says nothing about the order in which clients are served. Acting for the discretionary accounts before the recommendation change reaches everyone else denies the firm's other clients fair and impartial treatment, which Standard III(B) requires.

questions.stem: Hockett and Lopez meet the Kochanskis, a retired couple aged 61 with $7.4 million to invest, who explain during the meeting that they do not know enough about markets to manage their own investments. Hockett and Lopez take them through a presentation and explain why a balanced portfolio is best suited to them. The conduct of Hockett and Lopez is most likely a violation of:

options.A: Suitability.
options.B: Performance Presentation.
options.C: No Standard.

rationales.A: By developing and recommending a balanced portfolio for the Kochanskis without knowing their investment objectives, risk tolerance, horizon, and so on, Hockett and Lopez violated Standard III(C) Suitability. They must make a reasonable inquiry into a client's investment experience, risk and return objectives, and financial constraints prior to making any investment recommendation. They should have developed an investment policy statement for the Kochanskis before they recommended any investments; learning at the meeting only that the couple feel unable to manage their own money is not such an inquiry.
rationales.B: Standard III(D) Performance Presentation requires that communications about investment performance be fair, accurate, and complete, and nothing in the meeting suggests performance was misstated, even though returns featured in the presentation. The failure is one of sequence: a recommendation was developed and delivered before any reasonable inquiry into the clients' circumstances, which is Standard III(C).
rationales.C: A balanced portfolio may well prove reasonable for a retired couple, but suitability in the abstract cannot substitute for knowing these clients' objectives, risk tolerance, horizon, experience, and constraints before recommending anything. Standard III(C) requires the inquiry first, documented in an investment policy statement, and that inquiry had not been made.

questions.stem: BankGlobal Case — Lopez presentation of past performance information: uses average of four funds' five-year annualized returns labeled 'total portfolio return'; shows composite portfolio consisting of team's discretionary accounts of similar size, EXCLUDING terminated accounts. Most likely violation caused by:

options.A: Selecting discretionary accounts of similar size to build the composite was the violation.
options.B: Using an average of the four funds' returns to represent the model portfolio's performance was the violation. That specification would be used as-is, with no forward-looking overlay. Applied uniformly, it would bind at every horizon and every asset class.
options.C: Excluding terminated accounts — Lopez violated Standard III(D) Performance Presentation in her use and presentation of the composite portfolio's performance because she did NOT include the performance of TERMINATED ACCOUNTS.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Similar-size discretionary accounts are an appropriate composite population; the defect is EXCLUDING TERMINATED accounts, inflating the record.
rationales.B: Incorrect. For this novice audience, an average of the four funds is an acceptable simplification — the audience-tailoring principle.
rationales.C:
Full statement: Excluding terminated accounts — Lopez violated Standard III(D) Performance Presentation in her use and presentation of the composite portfolio's performance because she did NOT include the performance of TERMINATED ACCOUNTS; Lopez should have included terminated AND current discretionary accounts that were similar in her composite.

Correct. Per BankGlobal Case Solution: 'Lopez violated Standard III(D) Performance Presentation in her use and presentation of the composite portfolio's performance because she did not include the performance of terminated accounts. In addition, she included only the team's discretionary accounts of similar size to the Kochanskis'. Lopez should have included terminated and current discretionary accounts that were similar in her composite portfolio's performance. There is no need to include nondiscretionary accounts because clients make their own investment decisions for such accounts.'

questions.stem: BankGlobal Case — Hockett generating 'alpha' in conservative accounts: 90% of client accounts conservative with long-term objectives; generates short-term alpha by investing 15%–20% of portfolios in high-beta stocks that 'appear to have low risk'; no change in IPSs. Most likely violates:

options.A: There is no violation because high-beta stocks in modest proportion reduce overall portfolio risk through diversification.
options.B: Standard III(C) Suitability — Hockett is investing in high-beta stocks for client accounts with LONG-TERM OBJECTIVES in order to achieve his short-term quarterly performance bonus.
options.C: Hockett's conduct violates only Standard III(D) if the alpha is presented to prospects.

rationales.A: Incorrect. The 15% high-beta sleeve serves HIS short-term alpha objective, not the accounts' long-term conservative objectives — a suitability breach.
rationales.B:
Full statement: Standard III(C) Suitability — Hockett is investing in high-beta stocks for client accounts with LONG-TERM OBJECTIVES in order to achieve his short-term quarterly performance bonus; per Standard III(C), when responsible for managing a portfolio to a specific mandate, strategy, or style, must make only investment recommendations or take only investment actions that are CONSISTENT with the stated objectives and constraints; high-beta stocks by their very nature HAVE RISK; the high-beta stocks are contrary to the long-term risk profile established in the clients' IPSs; Hockett changed the investment strategy in an attempt to gain short-term rewards from firm's new compensation arrangement and not in response to changes in investment needs.

Correct. Per BankGlobal Case Solution: 'Hockett is violating Standard III(C) Suitability by investing in high-beta stocks for client accounts with long-term objectives in order to achieve his short-term quarterly performance bonus... High-beta stocks by their very nature have risk. Hockett is also violating Standard III(C) by investing 15%-20% of his clients' portfolios in high-beta stocks that "appear low risk." These high-beta stocks are contrary to the long-term risk profile established in the clients' investment policy statements (IPSs). Hockett changed the investment strategy for his clients in an attempt to reap short-term rewards offered by his firm's new compensation arrangement and not in response to changes in their investment needs.'
rationales.C: Incorrect. Presentation aside, investing inconsistently with client IPSs violates III(C) directly.

questions.stem: BankGlobal Case — Lopez social media post: after work Lopez posts to old high school friends: 'Just opened an account for Mr. Kochanski and his wife.' Most likely violates:

options.A: There is no violation because the audience was limited to old high school friends rather than the public. That specification would be used as-is, with no forward-looking overlay. Applied uniformly, it would bind at every horizon and every asset class.
options.B: Standard III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality — members must keep information about current, former, and prospective clients confidential unless: (1) info concerns illegal activities.
options.C: There is no violation because the post revealed no investment details or account balances.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Audience size does not matter; disclosure to anyone outside authorized colleagues breaches confidentiality.
rationales.B:
Full statement: Standard III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality — members must keep information about current, former, and prospective clients confidential unless: (1) info concerns illegal activities; (2) disclosure is required by law; or (3) the client permits disclosure; Standard III(E) requires that EVEN THE PRESENCE OF A CLIENT ACCOUNT be kept confidentially within the firm unless the client has been informed and has consented to the disclosure of the information; confidentiality extends BEYOND the investment industry to the population as a whole.

Correct. Per BankGlobal Case Solution: 'Lopez violated Standard III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality by posting about the Kochanskis' opening of an account... Standard III(E) requires that even the presence of a client account be kept confidentially within the firm unless the client has been informed and has consented to the disclosure of the information.'
rationales.C: Incorrect. The EXISTENCE of the client relationship is itself confidential information under III(E).

questions.stem: Castle Bio 1 — Plume not disclosing Global's ownership by Castle: Plume writes research reports on STRX/APBX (subsidiaries of Castle Biotechnology) but does not disclose in his research reports that Global (his employer) is owned by Castle. Most likely violates:

options.A: There is no violation because the ownership relationship is publicly disclosed in the subsidiaries' prospectuses.
options.B: The failure is one of independence under Standard I(B), since Castle's ownership pressures Plume's conclusions.
options.C: Standard VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts — by not disclosing that Global is owned by Castle in his research report, Plume violates VI(A).

rationales.A: Incorrect. Public availability elsewhere does not satisfy VI(A) — the conflict must be disclosed IN THE RESEARCH REPORT itself.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Pressure may exist, but the tested defect is the missing conflict disclosure in his reports.
rationales.C:
Full statement: Standard VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts — by not disclosing that Global is owned by Castle in his research report, Plume violates VI(A); CB's ownership of Global and Plume's close relationships with CB's management raise questions about Plume's ability to remain independent and objective; the fact that relationships are disclosed in offering prospectuses is NECESSARY BUT NOT SUFFICIENT to meet Standard VI(A) because they may not communicate the information effectively or in a prominent manner.

Correct. Per Castle Bio 1 Solution: 'By not disclosing that Global is owned by Castle in his research report, Plume is in violation of Standard VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts... CB's ownership of Global and Plume's close relationships with CB's management raise questions about Plume's ability to remain independent and objective... The fact that the relationships between Plume, CB, its subsidiaries, and Global are disclosed in the offering prospectus is necessary but not sufficient to meet Standard VI(A) because they may not communicate the information effectively or in a prominent manner.'

questions.stem: Castle Bio 1 — Plume not disclosing his ownership of CB Class A preferred shares and CB common stock options: Plume owns CB preferred shares and options granted while employee; does not own STRX/APBX shares directly. Most likely violates:

options.A: There is no violation because preferred shares and options confer no beneficial interest in the subsidiaries. That specification would be used as-is, with no forward-looking overlay. Applied uniformly, it would bind at every horizon and every asset class.
options.B: There is no violation because Plume owns no shares of STRX or APBX, the companies he covers.
options.C: Standard VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts — Plume's ownership of CB's preferred shares and stock options, along with CB's voting control of each company, gives him a BENEFICIAL OWNERSHIP INTEREST in STRX and APBX.

rationales.A: Incorrect. The indirect pecuniary link through the parent is precisely what VI(A) requires him to disclose.
rationales.B: Incorrect. His CB securities plus CB's voting control of the subsidiaries create an INDIRECT beneficial interest in the covered companies.
rationales.C:
Full statement: Standard VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts — Plume's ownership of CB's preferred shares and stock options, along with CB's voting control of each company, gives him a BENEFICIAL OWNERSHIP INTEREST in STRX and APBX; for the purposes of Standard VI(A), members and candidates BENEFICIALLY OWN securities if they have a DIRECT OR INDIRECT PECUNIARY INTEREST, have the POWER TO DIRECT VOTING, or have the POWER TO DISPOSE.

Correct. Per Castle Bio 1 Solution: 'By not disclosing his ownership of CB's preferred shares and stock options in his research report, Plume is in violation of Standard VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts. Because of this ownership in CB, Plume has a beneficial ownership interest in the securities of STRX and APBX, both of which he recommended as "buys." The most obvious conflict that must always be disclosed involves relationships between an issuer and the member, the candidate, or his or her firm. For the purposes of Standard VI(A), members and candidates beneficially own securities or other investments if they have a direct or indirect pecuniary interest in the securities, have the power to direct the voting of the shares of the securities or investments, or have the power to dispose of or direct the disposition of the security or investment.'

questions.stem: Castle Bio 1 — Plume's annual bonus based on IPO gross proceeds: bonus equal to 0.10% of gross proceeds for each IPO he works on with corporate finance department; not disclosed in his research report. Most likely violates:

options.A: The arrangement implicates only Standard VI(A) and is cured by disclosure in the research reports.
options.B: There is no violation because bonus arrangements tied to firm revenues are standard sell-side compensation.
options.C: Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity — members must use reasonable care and judgment to achieve and maintain independence and objectivity.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Disclosure helps, but compensation structurally linked to banking success attacks independence itself — I(B) is the operative standard.
rationales.B: Incorrect. A bonus tied to IPO proceeds he works on gives Plume a direct stake in banking outcomes — compromising research independence under I(B).
rationales.C:
Full statement: Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity — members must use reasonable care and judgment to achieve and maintain independence and objectivity; must NOT accept any gift, benefit, compensation, or consideration that reasonably could be expected to COMPROMISE independence and objectivity; compensation arrangements should NOT LINK analyst remuneration DIRECTLY to investment banking assignments in which the analysts may participate as a team member; Global can avoid the conflict by REMOVING this incentive from Plume's compensation package.

Correct. Per Castle Bio 1 Solution: 'By not disclosing his annual bonus in his research report, Plume is in violation of Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity... The guidance for Standard I(B) states, "Compensation arrangements should not link analyst remuneration directly to investment banking assignments in which the analysts may participate as a team member." The guidance also states, "Having analysts work with investment bankers is appropriate only when the conflicts are adequately and effectively managed and disclosed... Firms should require public disclosure of actual conflicts of interest to investors." Global can avoid the conflict by removing this incentive from Plume's compensation package.'

questions.stem: Castle Bio 1 — Plume selling APBX short in personal portfolio: three months after issuing 'buy' rec on APBX, Plume sells APBX short in personal portfolio; does not disclose because he was 'never a beneficial owner of APBX.' Most likely violates:

options.A: Standard VI(A) — selling APBX short in his personal portfolio while having a 'buy' recommendation on the stock is a conflict of interest that Plume needs to disclose.
options.B: There is no violation because analysts may manage personal portfolios according to their own risk views.
options.C: There is no violation because a short position is not beneficial ownership of the security.

rationales.A:
Full statement: Standard VI(A) — selling APBX short in his personal portfolio while having a 'buy' recommendation on the stock is a conflict of interest that Plume needs to disclose; Global could avoid this conflict by PROHIBITING such transactions by its employees; Plume's ownership of CB's preferred shares and common stock options, along with CB's voting control, gives him a beneficial ownership interest in APBX.

Correct. Per Castle Bio 1 Solution: 'By selling APBX short in his personal portfolio, Plume is in violation of Standard VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts... Selling APBX short in his personal portfolio while having a "buy" recommendation on the stock is a conflict of interest that Plume needs to disclose. Global could avoid this conflict by prohibiting such transactions by its employees.'
rationales.B: Incorrect. Holding a personal SHORT against his own outstanding BUY recommendation is a conflict that must be disclosed — personal risk views do not erase it.
rationales.C: Incorrect. A short position is a direct pecuniary interest in the covered security's decline; the conflict is real and disclosable.

questions.stem: Castle Bio 2 — Benning using social media/email to solicit former Kodiak clients after leaving: uses personal social media platforms and email to contact clients to inform them of her departure and solicit them to follow her to Global AFTER she resigned. Most likely:

options.A: Violates Standard IV(A) Loyalty — because Benning developed these client relationships while employed at Kodiak, soliciting the clients to follow her to Global breaches her duty of loyalty even after her resignation.
options.B: NO violation — Benning's solicitation of former clients via social media does not violate the Code and Standards.
options.C: Violates Standard III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality — the identities of Kodiak's clients are confidential firm information that Benning may not use to contact them after her departure.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Per the guidance to Standard IV(A) Loyalty, once employment with the former firm has ended, the standard does NOT prohibit former employees from contacting clients of their previous firm, as long as the contact information does not come from the former employer's records or from work performed for it and no applicable agreement is violated. Benning contacted the clients through her personal social media platforms and email AFTER she resigned, so no loyalty duty was breached.
rationales.B:
Full statement: NO violation — Benning's solicitation of former clients via social media does not violate the Code and Standards; per guidance to Standard IV(A) Loyalty, once employment with the former firm has ended, the standard does NOT prohibit former employees from CONTACTING CLIENTS of their previous firm as long as the contact information does not come from the records of or as a result of work for their former employer or such outreach does not violate an applicable agreement with the former firm.

Correct. Per Castle Bio 2 Solution: 'Benning's solicitation of former clients via social media does not violate the Code and Standards. The guidance to Standard IV(A) Loyalty states that once employment with the former firm has ended, the standard does not prohibit former employees from contacting clients of their previous firm as long as the contact information does not come from the records of as a result of work for their former employer or such outreach does not violate an applicable agreement with the former firm. Benning's employment with Kodak ended once she resigned, left the firm and no longer has responsibilities or is being paid by the firm.'

options.B: Balmer violated IV(C) by relying on the account review with Graeme instead of restricting his activities during the investigation. That specification would be used as-is, with no forward-looking overlay.
options.C: NO violation — as soon as she was made aware of the complaint, Balmer initiated an INVESTIGATION by calling Graeme into her office.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Her prompt investigation — calling Graeme in and reviewing the account and IPS — is exactly the reasonable supervisory response; board escalation is not the first step.
rationales.B: Incorrect. IV(C) requires the supervisor to promptly INITIATE AN ASSESSMENT of the possible wrongdoing — which Balmer did by calling Graeme in and sitting in on the review of Milgram's account and IPS; restricting an employee's activities is a response reserved for ongoing or likely continuing wrongdoing, not a prerequisite of every inquiry.
rationales.C:
Full statement: NO violation — as soon as she was made aware of the complaint, Balmer initiated an INVESTIGATION by calling Graeme into her office; she sat in on the meeting where Graeme reviewed Milgram's account and IPS; per IV(C), once a supervisor learns that an employee has violated or may have violated the C&S, the supervisor must promptly INITIATE AN ASSESSMENT to determine the extent of the wrongdoing; relying on employee's statements or assurances is NOT enough — Balmer's active investigation meets IV(C).

Correct. Per Milgram Solution: 'Balmer did not violate the Code and Standards. As soon as she was made aware of the complaint, she initiated an investigation by calling Graeme into her office. She sat in on the meeting, where Graeme reviewed Milgram's account and IPS. According to Standard IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors... once a supervisor learns that an employee has violated or may have violated the law or the Code and Standards, the supervisor must promptly initiate an assessment to determine the extent of the wrongdoing. Relying on an employee's statements about the extent of the violation or assurances that the wrongdoing will not reoccur is not enough.'

questions.stem: GHB Case — Yousoff not disclosing fee-sharing arrangement in MOU: Yousoff/Wong decide to pay Tan and Chuong (board members who built relationship with MGM2) a portion of MGM2's advisory fees; not disclosed in the MOU. Most likely:

options.A: The arrangement violates Standard VI(C) as an undisclosed referral fee paid to Tan and Chuong. That specification would be used as-is, with no forward-looking overlay.
options.B: NO violation — the fee-sharing arrangement is a REWARD paid to Tan and Chuong for their efforts to bring MGM2 on as a client.
options.C: The arrangement violates Standard VI(A) as an unmanaged conflict of interest within the MOU.

rationales.A: Incorrect. The payment rewards board members' business-development efforts on a won mandate — compensation for their work, not a client-referral fee.
rationales.B:
Full statement: NO violation — the fee-sharing arrangement is a REWARD paid to Tan and Chuong for their efforts to bring MGM2 on as a client; the fee arrangement is NOT a referral fee; Tan and Chuong did not refer MGM2 to GHB; a referral fee is compensation for the RECOMMENDATION of products or services; case facts provide no evidence that a conflict of interest is present.

Correct. Per GHB Case Solution: 'Yousoff is not in violation of the Code and Standards. The fee-sharing arrangement is a reward paid to Tan and Chuong for their efforts to bring MGM2 on as a client. The fee arrangement is not a referral fee. Tan and Chuong did not refer MGM2 to GHB. A referral fee is compensation, consideration, or benefit received from or paid to others for the recommendation of products or services.'
rationales.C: Incorrect. As structured, the reward arrangement is legitimate compensation; no violation arises from the MOU itself.

questions.stem: GHB Case — Chuong not disclosing information about her son to Yousoff: Hie (who helped found MGM2) recently hired Chuong's son in executive role. Most likely violates:

options.A: The failure is Standard I(C), because staying silent misrepresents Chuong's relationships to the firm.
options.B: Standard VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts — Hie's hiring of Chuong's son in an executive position at Hie's firm could reasonably be expected to IMPAIR Chuong's independence and objectivity with respect to interactions between MGM2 and GHB.
options.C: There is no violation because a son's employment is his own affair, not his mother's disclosure obligation. That specification would be used as-is, with no forward-looking overlay. Applied uniformly, it would bind at every horizon and every asset class.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Silence here is an undisclosed CONFLICT, not an affirmative misrepresentation.
rationales.B:
Full statement: Standard VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts — Hie's hiring of Chuong's son in an executive position at Hie's firm could reasonably be expected to IMPAIR Chuong's independence and objectivity with respect to interactions between MGM2 and GHB; VI(A) requires Chuong to disclose this conflict.

Correct. Per GHB Case Solution: 'Hie's hiring of Chuong's son in an executive position at Hie's firm could reasonably be expected to impair Chuong's independence and objectivity with respect to interactions between MGM2 and GHB. Standard VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts requires Chuong to disclose this conflict.'
rationales.C: Incorrect. Hie hiring her son into an executive role could reasonably impair Chuong's objectivity toward Hie's business — a disclosable VI(A) conflict.

questions.stem: GHB Case — Sim destroying documentation of meeting with Hie at his request: uses fact sheet Hie provided to prepare IPS; destroys other notes she took during meeting. Most likely violates:

options.A: There is no violation because the fact sheet Hie provided is the official record and Sim's personal notes are duplicative working papers. That specification would be used as-is, with no forward-looking overlay.
options.B: There is no violation because destroying the notes honored the client's confidentiality request.
options.C: Standard V(C) Record Retention — members must develop and maintain APPROPRIATE RECORDS to support their investment analyses, recommendations, actions, and other investment-related communications.

rationales.A: Incorrect. The notes are not duplicative — V(C)'s guidance lists notes from clients among the supporting records that substantiate the scope of research and the reasons for actions; by destroying all notes from the meeting, Sim fails to maintain appropriate records supporting her investment actions.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Confidentiality protects information from outsiders; it does not authorize destroying records that support the IPS and advice.
rationales.C:
Full statement: Standard V(C) Record Retention — members must develop and maintain APPROPRIATE RECORDS to support their investment analyses, recommendations, actions, and other investment-related communications; some examples of supporting documentation include notes from clients; by destroying all notes from their meeting, Sim is not maintaining appropriate records to support her investment actions.

Correct. Per GHB Case Solution: 'Sim violated Standard V(C) Record Retention: "Members and Candidates must develop and maintain appropriate records to support their investment analyses, recommendations, actions, and other investment-related communications with clients and prospective clients." The guidance for Standard V(C) states, "Members and candidates must retain records that substantiate the scope of their research and reasons for their actions or conclusions." Some examples of supporting documentation include notes from clients. By destroying all notes from their meeting, Sim is not maintaining appropriate records to support her investment actions.'

questions.stem: GHB Case — Sim not disclosing Hie's promised year-end bonus to Yousoff: Hie promises Sim a bonus at year-end if she processes transactions in a timely manner. Most likely violates:

options.A: Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements — members must NOT accept gifts, benefits, compensation, or consideration that competes with or might reasonably be expected to create a conflict of interest with their employer's interest UNLESS they obtain written consent from all parties involved.
options.B: The promised bonus violates Standard VI(A) as an undisclosed conflict of interest that Sim was required to disclose prominently to all of her other clients.
options.C: There is no violation because a bonus offered by a grateful client is a personal gift rather than compensation, and gifts from clients fall entirely outside the scope of the additional-compensation standard.

rationales.A:
Full statement: Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements — members must NOT accept gifts, benefits, compensation, or consideration that competes with or might reasonably be expected to create a conflict of interest with their employer's interest UNLESS they obtain written consent from all parties involved; Hie's promise of a bonus if Sim processes his transactions in a timely manner could conflict with Sim's responsibilities to her other clients or other clients of GHB; at a minimum, Sim must disclose the bonus arrangement to Yousoff, her employer.

Correct. Per GHB Case Solution: 'By not disclosing her bonus arrangement with Hie, Sim violated the Code and Standards. According to Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements, "Members and Candidates must not accept gifts, benefits, compensation, or consideration that competes with or might reasonably be expected to create a conflict of interest with their employer's interest unless they obtain written consent from all parties involved." Hie's promise of a bonus if Sim processes his transactions in a timely manner could conflict with Sim's responsibilities to her other clients or other clients of GHB.'
rationales.B: Incorrect. The operative failure is the undisclosed additional-compensation arrangement with the employer, governed by IV(B).
rationales.C: Incorrect. A promised year-end bonus contingent on service creates an arrangement that can conflict with the employer's interest — IV(B) requires written consent before acceptance.

questions.stem: GHB Case — Sim opening Hie's account without full inquiry: Hie refuses to answer risk tolerance, objectives, experience questions saying he'll invest in short-term US govt securities initially; Sim uses his fact sheet and opens the account. Most likely violates:

options.A: There is no violation because short-term government securities carry effectively no risk of unsuitability.
options.B: Standard III(C) Suitability — Sim did not complete the required section on Hie's investment experience, objectives, and risk tolerance of new clients.
options.C: There is no violation because Hie explicitly declined to answer the questions, and a client may waive the suitability inquiry.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Suitability information — experience, objectives, risk tolerance — is required AT INCEPTION regardless of how safe the initial investment seems.
rationales.B:
Full statement: Standard III(C) Suitability — Sim did not complete the required section on Hie's investment experience, objectives, and risk tolerance of new clients; the information Hie provided was NOT SUFFICIENT for Sim to develop an appropriate IPS; the standard requires when an advisory relationship exists, members and candidates must GATHER CLIENT INFORMATION at the inception of the relationship; a client's statement regarding his or her desired investment strategy, especially without a fully formed IPS, does not meet the requirements of III(C).

Correct. Per GHB Case Solution: 'Sim did not complete the required section on Hie's investment experience, objectives, and risk tolerance of new clients; the information Hie provided was not sufficient for Sim to develop an appropriate IPS. Sim violated Standard III(C) Suitability. The standard requires that when an advisory relationship exists, members and candidates must gather client information at the inception of the relationship.'
rationales.C: Incorrect. A client cannot waive the inception inquiry — III(C) requires members in an advisory relationship to gather information on investment experience, objectives, and risk tolerance at the inception of the relationship, and Hie's fact sheet was not sufficient for Sim to develop an appropriate IPS.

questions.stem: GHB Case — first course of action after Yousoff dismisses Sim's money-laundering concerns: Sim believes Hie may be using account to launder money; Yousoff dismisses concerns. Sim should:

options.A: Take no action since she has informed Yousoff of her concerns.
options.B: Contact the regulator in her jurisdiction.
options.C: Contact GHB's compliance department.

rationales.A: Insufficient action.
rationales.B: Regulator not first step.
rationales.C:
Full statement: Contact GHB's compliance department — per guidance to Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law: 'When in doubt about the appropriate action to undertake, it is recommended that a member or candidate seek the advice of compliance personnel or legal counsel concerning legal requirements. If a potential violation is being committed by a fellow employee, it may also be prudent for the member or candidate to seek the advice of the firm's compliance department or legal counsel.'

Correct. Per GHB Case Solution: 'The guidance for Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law states, "When in doubt about the appropriate action to undertake, it is recommended that a member or candidate seek the advice of compliance personnel or legal counsel concerning legal requirements. If a potential violation is being committed by a fellow employee, it may also be prudent for the member or candidate to seek the advice of the firm's compliance department or legal counsel."'

questions.stem: GHB Case — Sim recommending oil-linked structured note to Madam Tan: Madam Tan (70, retired seamstress) wants to invest in conservative equities for grandchildren's education; heard about oil-linked structured note from friends; Sim summarizes verbally; Madam Tan admits she is unsure what oil futures are or how they work but decides to put $50,000 in. Most likely violates:

options.A: Standard III(C) Suitability — structured notes are UNSUITABLE for Madam Tan.
options.B: No violation — the note was a client-initiated, unsolicited request, so responsibility for its suitability shifted to Madam Tan.
options.C: No violation — Sim verbally summarized the note's features and risks before Madam Tan decided to invest.

rationales.A:
Full statement: Standard III(C) Suitability — structured notes are UNSUITABLE for Madam Tan; Madam Tan has previously invested in real estate; since retiring has invested in fixed deposits and lower-risk energy utility stocks; she now wishes to invest more in CONSERVATIVE equities; she is unsure what oil futures are or how they work; members and candidates need to make reasonable efforts to BALANCE clients' trading requests with their responsibilities to follow the agreed-on investment policy statement.

Correct. Per GHB Case Solution: 'Sim violated Standard III(C) Suitability. The structured notes are unsuitable for Madam Tan. Although Madam Tan has previously invested in real estate, since retiring, she has invested in fixed deposits and lower-risk energy utility stocks. She now wishes to invest more of her portfolio in conservative equites. In addition, Madam Tan shares that she is unsure what oil futures are or how they work... Members and candidates need to make reasonable efforts to balance their clients' trading requests with their responsibilities to follow the agreed-on investment policy statement.'
rationales.B: Incorrect. A client-initiated request does not eliminate suitability duties — members and candidates must make reasonable efforts to BALANCE clients' trading requests with their responsibility to follow the agreed-on IPS, and Madam Tan's conservative profile makes the structured note unsuitable under III(C).
rationales.C: Incorrect. A verbal summary does not cure unsuitability — Madam Tan admits she is unsure what oil futures are or how they work, and the note conflicts with her conservative objectives, so Sim still violated III(C).

questions.stem: GHB Case — Sim speaking with Tan and Chuong about Hie's account: Hie has told Sim to seek information as needed from board members Tan and Chuong. Most likely:

options.A: NO violation — per Standard III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality, a member or candidate can BREAK CONFIDENCE when permission is granted by the client.
options.B: Discussing Hie's account with Tan and Chuong violates Standard III(E) confidentiality.
options.C: Sim may share information with Tan and Chuong only if Hie's permission is documented in writing, which he did not provide.

rationales.A:
Full statement: NO violation — per Standard III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality, a member or candidate can BREAK CONFIDENCE when permission is granted by the client; in this case, Hie has given his permission to Sim by telling her to seek information as needed from board members Tan and Chuong, so Sim is NOT in violation.

Correct. Per GHB Case Solution: 'According to the standard, then, a member or candidate can break confidence when permission is granted by the client. In this case, Hie has given his permission to Sim by telling her to seek information as needed from board members Tan and Chuong, so Sim is not in violation of the Code and Standards.'
rationales.B: Incorrect. Hie GRANTED PERMISSION to consult the board members — client-authorized sharing is an express exception to confidentiality.
rationales.C: Incorrect. III(E) turns on client permission, not on any particular form of it — Hie's instruction to seek information as needed from board members Tan and Chuong is a grant of permission, so Sim is not in violation.

questions.stem: Ethical Decision-Making Framework per Exhibit 1 most likely consists of:

options.A: The framework consists of: (1) IDENTIFY: relevant facts, stakeholders and duties owed, ethical principles, conflicts of interest; (2) CONSIDER: situational influences, additional guidance, alternative actions; (3) DECIDE AND ACT; (4) REFLECT: was the outcome as anticipated? Why or why not?
options.B: The Ethical Decision-Making Framework is a compliance checklist applied only after a violation is suspected.
options.C: The framework consists of Identify, Consider, and Decide and Act — concluding once the action is taken, with no reflection phase.

rationales.A:
Full statement: the framework consists of: (1) IDENTIFY: relevant facts, stakeholders and duties owed, ethical principles, conflicts of interest; (2) CONSIDER: situational influences, additional guidance, alternative actions; (3) DECIDE AND ACT; (4) REFLECT: was the outcome as anticipated? Why or why not?; the framework's components do NOT need to be addressed in the sequence shown, but a REVIEW OF THE OUTCOME should conclude the process; this review provides insights for improved decision making in the future.

Correct. Per Exhibit 1: A Framework for Ethical Decision Making: 'Identify: Relevant facts, stakeholders and duties owed, ethical principles, conflicts of interest. Consider: Situational influences, additional guidance, alternative actions. Decide and act. Reflect: Was the outcome as anticipated? Why or why not?' Per the introduction: 'The framework's components do not need to be addressed in the sequence shown, but a review of the outcome should conclude the process. This review provides insights for improved decision making in the future.'
rationales.B: Incorrect. It is a prospective decision aid — Identify, Consider, Decide and Act, Reflect — not a post hoc audit tool.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The framework has FOUR phases — although the components need not be addressed in the sequence shown, a REVIEW OF THE OUTCOME (Reflect) should conclude the process, providing insights for improved decision making in the future.

drills.los_text: explain how the practices, policies, or conduct does or does not violate the CFA Institute Code of Ethics and Standards of Professional Conduct
drills.reading_name: Application of the Code and Standards: Level III

questions.stem: Adebayo's project sequencing decision — explanation of why V(A) violation most likely:

options.A: Adebayo could have satisfied V(A) by deferring the sequencing decision to a higher governmental authority.
options.B: Disclosing the political situational influences would have replaced Adebayo's need to exercise independent judgment. That specification would be used as-is, with no forward-looking overlay.
options.C: Adebayo faced political pressures from senior governmental supporters of each project.

rationales.A: Wrong — the curriculum states deferring to a higher governmental authority would not mitigate, and may in fact enhance, political influence on the decision.
rationales.B: Wrong — disclosing outside negative influences or conflicts does not replace the need to act with independent and objective judgment when selecting investments.
rationales.C:
Full statement: Adebayo faced political pressures from senior governmental supporters of each project; her 'quick' decision was made based on POLITICAL, not investment or financial, considerations; she must thoroughly and independently investigate each potential investment and be resolute in maintaining her independence and objectivity to act in the best interests of NI and its investors; deferring the decision to a higher governmental authority would NOT mitigate and may in fact ENHANCE political influence; disclosing outside negative situational influences or conflicts of interest does NOT replace the need to act with independent and objective judgment.

Correct. Per SIC Case Solution: 'Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis requires members to exercise diligence, independence, and thoroughness, as well as to have a reasonable and adequate basis to support investment action... deferring the decision to a higher governmental authority would not mitigate and may in fact enhance political influence on the investment decision rather than ensure each project is objectively considered for its individual investment merit... disclosing outside negative situational influences or conflicts of interest does not replace the need to act with independent and objective judgement when analyzing and selecting investment opportunities.'

questions.stem: Why NI's dual mandate makes Adebayo's high-return assurance a violation most likely:

options.A: In the case of NI, Adebayo has a DUAL MANDATE to invest in projects that have both a beneficial SOCIOECONOMIC IMPACT and a positive EXPECTED INVESTMENT RETURN.
options.B: The assurance was improper only because hedge funds are prohibited investors in development institutions.
options.C: The assurance was acceptable because sophisticated hedge fund investors understand that high-return commitments are aspirational rather than binding. That specification would be used as-is, with no forward-looking overlay.

rationales.A:
Full statement: in the case of NI, Adebayo has a DUAL MANDATE to invest in projects that have both a beneficial SOCIOECONOMIC IMPACT and a positive EXPECTED INVESTMENT RETURN; this dual mandate is in contrast to traditional investment mandates that focus only on ROI regardless of outside or other impact; NI's investors are informed up front that investment return is not the single determining factor for NI's investment decisions; therefore, any assurance promising a SET RATE OF RETURN or PRIORITIZING RETURN MAXIMIZATION would be contrary to the mandate and thus a III(C) Suitability violation.

Correct. Per SIC Case Solution: 'In the case of NI, Adebayo has a dual mandate to invest in projects that have both a beneficial socioeconomic impact and a positive expected investment return. This dual mandate is in contrast to traditional investment mandates that focus only on ROI regardless of outside or other impact. NI's investors are informed up front that investment return is not the single determining factor for NI's investment decisions. Any assurances by Adebayo to the hedge fund or other investors that promise a set rate of return or prioritize return maximization would be contrary to NI's mandate.'
rationales.B: Incorrect. No investor-class prohibition exists; the defect is promising returns inconsistent with the dual mandate.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Investor sophistication is no defense — NI's investors are informed up front that investment return is not the single determining factor for NI's decisions, so any assurance promising a set rate of return or prioritizing return maximization contradicts the dual mandate and violates III(C).

questions.stem: Why Corrales's personal investment is front-running most likely:

options.A: Corrales's trade is problematic only because he used hedge fund research in selecting NI.
options.B: Corrales's trade was acceptable because VI(B) permits personal trades that do not disadvantage the employer's fund in any way. That specification would be used as-is, with no forward-looking overlay.
options.C: After the hedge fund invests in NI, the value of NI shares increases, benefiting Corrales through an increase in the value of his personal investment.

rationales.A: Incorrect. The problem is sequence and benefit — buying before the fund so its investment lifts his shares — not research reuse.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The practice violates VI(B) EVEN IF his personal investment does not disadvantage the hedge fund — buying ahead of HFI's investment let Corrales capture for himself the price appreciation the fund's transaction produced; he should have waited until after the fund completed its investment.
rationales.C:
Full statement: after the hedge fund invests in NI, the value of NI shares increases, benefiting Corrales through an increase in the value of his personal investment; the practice is unethical and violates Standard VI(B) EVEN IF his personal investment does not disadvantage the hedge fund in any way; Corrales should have waited to invest in NI until AFTER the hedge fund had completed its investment; purchasing the same investments as your employer or investing in the same assets as your clients does not necessarily create a conflict of interest, although best practice recommends that such 'co-investing' be disclosed.

Correct. Per SIC Case Solution: 'After the hedge fund invests in NI, the value of NI shares increases, benefiting Corrales through an increase in the value of his personal investment. This practice is unethical and violates Standard VI(B) even if his personal investment does not disadvantage the hedge fund in any way. Corrales should have waited to invest in NI until after the hedge fund had completed its investment in NI... Purchasing the same investments as your employer or investing in the same assets as your clients does not necessarily create a conflict of interest, although best practice recommends that such "co-investing" be disclosed.'

questions.stem: Why Corrales's 'deal fees' violation is misrepresentation not diligence most likely:

options.A: The payments are acceptable local business practice under I(A) because the applicable law of the jurisdiction tolerates facilitation fees. That specification would be used as-is, with no forward-looking overlay. Applied uniformly, it would bind at every horizon and every asset class.
options.B: The reporting treatment is acceptable because operating expenses is a flexible accounting category.
options.C: Although it is acceptable to hire subadvisers to assist in sourcing investment opportunities, Corrales is NOT hiring a subadviser to assist in the investment decision-making process but is essentially engaged in BRIBERY and facilitating local corruption.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Local tolerance does not sanitize the conduct — the 'deal fees' are corrupt payments for official connections, unsupported by documentation of legitimate investment expenses and likely in violation of anti-bribery laws; labeling them operating expenses misrepresents them.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Flexibility in accounting labels cannot make connection payments into legitimate operating costs.
rationales.C:
Full statement: although it is acceptable to hire subadvisers to assist in sourcing investment opportunities, Corrales is NOT hiring a subadviser to assist in the investment decision-making process but is essentially engaged in BRIBERY and facilitating local corruption; the 'deal fees' are corrupt transactions and are not supported by any documentation that details legitimate investment expenses; investment advisers who hire subadvisers must ensure they have the necessary knowledge or expertise to meet the need for diligence and thoroughness — but the underlying violation here is not the delegation itself but the misrepresentation of corrupt payments as legitimate operating expenses.

Correct. Per SIC Case Solution: 'Although it is acceptable to hire subadvisers to assist in sourcing investment opportunities, Corrales is not hiring a subadviser to assist in the investment decision-making process but is essentially engaged in bribery and facilitating local corruption... The "deal fees" are corrupt transactions and are not supported by any documentation that details legitimate investment expenses. Corrales very likely violates Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law because his conduct would most likely violate applicable anti-bribery laws.'

questions.stem: Why CFA designation is not like a university degree most likely:

options.A: Unlike a university degree — once granted the right to use the designation, individuals must ALSO SATISFY CFA Institute membership requirements (including paying dues and submitting a Professional Conduct Statement annually) to maintain the right to refer to themselves as CFA charterholders.
options.B: The designation is exactly like a university degree: once the charter is earned, the right to use the letters is unconditional and permanent, surviving any lapse in dues or conduct filings. That is the precise misconception: unlike a degree, the designation requires annual maintenance (agreement, PCS, dues).
options.C: A lapsed member may continue using the CFA designation as long as she passed all three exams and intends to pay the back dues.

rationales.A:
Full statement: unlike a university degree — once granted the right to use the designation, individuals must ALSO SATISFY CFA Institute membership requirements (including paying dues and submitting a Professional Conduct Statement annually) to maintain the right to refer to themselves as CFA charterholders; because Adebayo has not been paying her CFA Institute dues, her membership is considered LAPSED; until membership is reactivated, she must NOT use the CFA designation or present herself as a charterholder, although she MAY state she was previously a CFA Institute member.

Correct. Per SIC Case Solution: 'The CFA designation is not like a degree from a university in that once granted the right to use the designation, individuals must also satisfy CFA Institute membership requirements (including paying dues and submitting a Professional Conduct Statement annually) to maintain the right to refer to themselves as CFA charterholders. Although Adebayo earned her charter, her membership is considered lapsed because she has not been paying her CFA Institute dues. Until her membership is reactivated, she must not use the CFA designation or present herself as a charterholder to potential investors, although she may state she was previously a CFA Institute member.'
rationales.B: Incorrect. That is the precise misconception: unlike a degree, the designation requires annual maintenance (agreement, PCS, dues).
rationales.C: Incorrect. Intent to pay is insufficient — because Adebayo has not been paying her dues, her membership is LAPSED, and until it is reactivated she must NOT use the CFA designation or present herself as a charterholder, although she may state she was previously a CFA Institute member.

questions.curriculum_ref: V5 LM9 — SIC Adebayo CFA rationale

questions.stem: Why Mehrotra's silence assists Adebayo's violation most likely:

options.A: Mehrotra's silence is acceptable because members must dissociate only from their own misconduct, not that of colleagues.
options.B: Mehrotra hears Adebayo refer to herself as a charterholder, but he KNOWS that her CFA Institute membership has lapsed.
options.C: Mehrotra made no false statement to the client himself, so no standard reaches his silence.

rationales.A: Wrong — Standard I(A) requires members to dissociate from any unethical or illegal conduct, including a colleague's, and prohibits knowingly assisting it.
rationales.B:
Full statement: Mehrotra hears Adebayo refer to herself as a charterholder, but he KNOWS that her CFA Institute membership has lapsed; Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law prohibits members from KNOWINGLY PARTICIPATING OR ASSISTING in the violations of others; by keeping silent about false information given to a potential investor when doing so is potentially harmful, Mehrotra's behavior constitutes ASSISTING in the violations even if there is no active conduct; BEST PRACTICE would be for Mehrotra to address Adebayo directly and ask her to reinstate her membership or correct the statement, and if she refuses, bring the conduct to SIC's compliance department and DISSOCIATE from future sales meetings.

Correct. Per SIC Case Solution: 'Mehrotra hears Adebayo refer to herself as a charterholder, but he knows that because Adebayo has not paid her dues, her CFA Institute membership has lapsed. Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law prohibits members from knowingly participating or assisting in the violations of others and requires members to dissociate from any unethical or illegal conduct... Best practice, although difficult, would be for Mehrotra to address Adebayo directly about her conduct and ask her to reinstate her membership or correct the statement made to the potential investor. If Adebayo refuses to take corrective action, Mehrotra could bring this conduct to the attention of the SIC's compliance department for them to address. Mehrotra should dissociate from the activity by not participating in any future sales meetings with Adebayo.'
rationales.C: Wrong — Standard I(A) prohibits knowingly participating or assisting in others' violations; silence that assists a colleague's misrepresentation is covered even without active conduct.

questions.stem: Why sharing exam difficulty opinions is OK but topic coverage is not most likely:

options.A: Candidates must keep all details of their exam experience confidential, so even general difficulty impressions may not be shared. That specification would be used as-is, with no forward-looking overlay.
options.B: Candidates may disclose which topic areas were or were not tested provided they omit the specific wording of questions.
options.C: Candidates may discuss their exam experience in GENERAL TERMS.

rationales.A: Wrong — overstates the confidentiality duty; Standard VII(A) permits candidates to discuss their exam experience in general terms, including relative difficulty.
rationales.B: Wrong — Standard VII(A) prohibits revealing specific subjects that are or are not tested, not merely question wording.
rationales.C:
Full statement: candidates may discuss their exam experience in GENERAL TERMS; they cannot provide specific information about the exam questions or curriculum subjects that ARE OR ARE NOT tested on the exam; a candidate saying the ethics topic in the exam was difficult is NOT in violation of Standard VII(A), but a candidate saying there were no exam questions on insider information would violate VII(A); Mehrotra soliciting information about specific exam questions to improve future preparatory classes violates VII(A).

Correct. Per SIC Case Solution: 'Candidates can discuss their exam experience in general terms. However, they cannot provide specific information about the exam questions or curriculum subjects that are or are not tested on the exam. Mehrotra cannot pass such information to future candidates without violating Standard VII(A). For example, although CFA Institute makes known to candidates that ethics is one of 10 topic areas tested on the exam, there may not be an exam question on the subject of material nonpublic information. A candidate saying the ethics topic in the exam was difficult is not in violation of Standard VII(A), but a candidate saying there were no exam questions on insider information would violate Standard VII(A).'

questions.stem: Why Hockett's team acting on rec changes for discretionary accounts is III(B) not II(A) most likely:

options.A: A pending in-house recommendation change is material nonpublic information, making this a Standard II(A) violation.
options.B: BankGlobal's recommendations are relied upon by the general investing public, so the team possessed material nonpublic information.
options.C: The research team develops their recommendations for management of ALL BankGlobal's client accounts.

questions.stem: Why fact sheet + risk-free securities does not satisfy III(C) at account inception most likely:

options.A: A client's statement regarding his or her desired investment strategy, especially WITHOUT a fully formed IPS, does not meet III(C) requirements.
options.B: A client's own strategy declaration always satisfies suitability requirements at inception.
options.C: The fact sheet satisfied III(C) because short-term government securities cannot be unsuitable for any investor.

rationales.A:
Full statement: a client's statement regarding his or her desired investment strategy, especially WITHOUT a fully formed IPS, does not meet III(C) requirements; the fact sheet does not provide enough information for Sim to develop an appropriate IPS; III(C) requires when an advisory relationship exists, members must GATHER CLIENT INFORMATION at the inception of the relationship, including financial circumstances, personal data (age, occupation) relevant to investment decisions, attitudes toward risk, and objectives; this information should be incorporated into a written IPS.

Per GHB Case Solution: 'A client's statement regarding his or her desired investment strategy, especially without a fully formed IPS, does not meet the requirements of Standard III(C) Suitability... The fact sheet does not provide enough information for Sim to develop an appropriate IPS... The standard requires that when an advisory relationship exists, members and candidates must gather client information at the inception of the relationship. rationales.B: Incorrect. A bare client declaration, without a formed IPS and inquiry, does not meet the inception requirements.
rationales.C: Incorrect. options.A: Sim may break confidence only when disclosure is required by law or concerns illegal activities, neither of which applies here. That specification would be used as-is, with no forward-looking overlay.
options.B: Per III(E), a member or candidate can BREAK CONFIDENCE when PERMISSION IS GRANTED BY THE CLIENT.
options.C: Standard III(E) permits no exceptions, so Sim may not discuss Hie's account with Tan and Chuong under any circumstances.

questions.stem: Why oil-linked structured note is unsuitable for Madam Tan most likely:

options.A: The note is unsuitable only because structured products are prohibited for retail investors.
options.B: A client-initiated request shifts suitability responsibility to the client, so Sim needed only to execute the trade accurately.
options.C: Structured notes are UNSUITABLE for Madam Tan — she has invested in fixed deposits and lower-risk energy utility stocks since retiring.

rationales.B: Incorrect. Although Madam Tan has previously invested in real estate, since retiring, she has invested in fixed deposits and lower-risk energy utility stocks. questions.stem: Purpose of the Ethical Decision-Making Framework per Exhibit 1 most likely:

options.A: The framework must be applied strictly in the sequence shown and concludes with Decide and Act, with no retrospective review.
options.B: The framework is a post hoc audit tool, applied after a decision has been made to determine whether the Code and Standards were violated. That specification would be used as-is, with no forward-looking overlay.
options.C: The framework is a useful framework to help NAVIGATE the ethical decision-making process and apply the Code and Standards.

rationales.A: Incorrect. The framework's components do NOT need to be addressed in the sequence shown, and a REVIEW OF THE OUTCOME (Reflect) should conclude the process — it does not end at Decide and Act.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The framework is a prospective aid for NAVIGATING ethical decisions as they are made and for applying the Code and Standards; the concluding Reflect step improves future decision making, but the framework is not an after-the-fact compliance audit.
rationales.C:
Full statement: the framework is a useful framework to help NAVIGATE the ethical decision-making process and apply the Code and Standards; the framework's components do not need to be addressed in the sequence shown, but a REVIEW OF THE OUTCOME should conclude the process; this review provides insights for IMPROVED DECISION MAKING in the future; the four steps are: Identify (relevant facts, stakeholders and duties owed, ethical principles, conflicts of interest); Consider (situational influences, additional guidance, alternative actions); Decide and act; Reflect (was the outcome as anticipated? Why or why not?).

Correct. Per Introduction and Exhibit 1: 'The purpose of this learning module is to provide examples of how the CFA Institute Code of Ethics and Standards of Professional Conduct (Code and Standards) can be applied in situations requiring professional and ethical judgment. Exhibit 1 presents a useful framework to help navigate the ethical decision-making process and apply the Code and Standards. The framework's components do not need to be addressed in the sequence shown, but a review of the outcome should conclude the process.
